title: Real-World Architectures
summary: Famous systems aren't magic — they're a few reusable patterns applied under brutal constraints. Learn the patterns and the why, not the brand names.

blocks.markdown:
Big systems are the same patterns under extreme pressure — interviewers reward the *why*, not the trivia.

- **Twitter** — feed fan-out: pay at write time or read time.
- **Netflix** — split a tiny control plane from a huge CDN data plane.
- **Uber** — shard the planet into cells, match locally.
- **WhatsApp** — millions of cheap connections, ruthless simplicity.
- **Google** — inverted index sharded by document, scatter-gather.
- **Stripe** — idempotency keys + an append-only ledger.

blocks.subTitle: Three meta-levers
blocks.markdown:
Every design here is an answer to the same three questions.

- **Where do you do the work?** At write time or read time.
- **How do you partition state?** By user, geography, or document.
- **How do you survive failure?** Retries, idempotency, redundancy.

Great architecture makes the common operation cheap and keeps running when parts die.

blocks.subTitle: Twitter — timeline fan-out
blocks.markdown:
Building each home timeline fast is the hard part — and there are two ways.

![Twitter fan-out on write versus on read](assets/real-world-architectures/twitter-fanout.svg)

- **Fan-out-on-write (push)** — on tweet, insert into every follower's precomputed list. Reads are trivial; writes explode for big accounts.
- **Fan-out-on-read (pull)** — store the tweet once, merge followees live at read time. Cheap writes, expensive reads.
- Reads outnumber writes ~40:1, so paying at write time usually wins. See [caching](caching).

assets.alt: Twitter fan-out on write versus on read

blocks.subTitle: Twitter — the hybrid
blocks.markdown:
Pure push breaks on celebrities, so Twitter goes hybrid.

- A 50M-follower tweet means 50M list inserts — a write storm.
- **Push for normal accounts**, but skip pre-fan-out above a follower threshold.
- At read time, merge your precomputed timeline with the latest from the few celebrities you follow.
- This caps worst-case write amplification while keeping the common read cheap. The breaking parameter is **follower count**.

blocks.subTitle: Netflix — control vs data plane
blocks.markdown:
Netflix splits into two physically separate planes.

![Netflix control plane on AWS plus Open Connect CDN](assets/real-world-architectures/netflix-edge.svg)

- **Control plane** — ~1000 microservices on AWS decide *what* to play; an edge gateway (Zuul) routes requests.
- **Data plane** — video bytes stream from **Open Connect** boxes inside your ISP, never through the microservices.
- Each service has a **circuit breaker** so a slow dependency fails fast with a fallback. See [monolith-microservices](monolith-microservices).

assets.alt: Netflix control plane on AWS plus Open Connect CDN

blocks.subTitle: Uber — geospatial sharding
blocks.markdown:
You can't scan every driver on Earth per request, so Uber partitions space.

![Uber dispatch with geospatial cell sharding](assets/real-world-architectures/uber-dispatch.svg)

- Convert lat/lng into a grid **cell** (H3 hexagons — every neighbor is equidistant).
- **Shard driver state by cell**; route a request to the node owning the rider's cell and search that cell plus neighbors.
- Drivers ping location every ~4s to keep the in-memory index fresh.
- The pain: **hot cells** (airports, concerts) need rebalancing and surge. See [nosql-distributed-data](nosql-distributed-data).

assets.alt: Uber dispatch with geospatial cell sharding

blocks.subTitle: WhatsApp & Google
blocks.markdown:
Two more constraints, two more partition choices.

- **WhatsApp** — the constraint is *open connections*. Erlang gives millions of cheap lightweight processes plus supervision, so each connection is one tiny process. ~50 engineers ran ~900M users.
- **Google Search** — an **inverted index** (word → documents) sharded by document. A query **scatter-gathers** to all shards in parallel and merges the top-N. See [search-indexing](search-indexing).

blocks.subTitle: Stripe — idempotency & ledger
blocks.markdown:
Payments live and die by two ideas: safe retries and immutable money.

```python
def charge(req):
    key = req.idempotency_key       # client-generated, one per logical charge
    if seen := store.get(key):
        return seen                 # retry returns the stored result
    result = do_charge(req)
    store.put(key, result)
    return result
```

- **Idempotency key** turns at-least-once delivery into exactly-once *effect*.
- **Double-entry ledger** — money is append-only; balances are a *sum* of immutable entries, never overwritten. See [event-driven-cqrs](event-driven-cqrs).

blocks.subTitle: Pick the pattern for the problem
blocks.markdown:
Map the problem to the system that solved it.

| Problem | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Feed at scale | Push vs read fan-out, hybrid |
| Heavy bytes globally | Control + CDN data plane |
| Find nearest X | Geo cells, shard by cell |
| Millions of connections | Lightweight concurrency |
| Money correctness | Idempotency + ledger |

blocks.subTitle: The levers you trade
blocks.markdown:
Each system trades the same dials differently.

- **Read cost vs write cost** — precompute (cheap reads, heavy writes) or compute on read. Decide on your read:write ratio.
- **Latency vs freshness** — a CDN or replica is fast but may be stale; strong consistency is correct but slower.
- **Simplicity vs flexibility** — WhatsApp's lean stack vs Netflix's 1000 services and their ops tax.
- **Cost of failure** — a stale feed is fine; a double charge is a lawsuit. Higher cost buys more consistency machinery.

blocks.subTitle: Why each company built it
blocks.markdown:
The constraint forced the design in every case.

- **Netflix** built its own CDN because it is a huge share of internet bytes — owning delivery beats renting.
- **Uber** open-sourced H3 and Ringpop because geography is the natural partition key for ride-hailing.
- **Stripe** optimizes exactly-once effect and audit over throughput because money's cost-of-error is extreme.
- **WhatsApp** matched the runtime to one constraint and kept scope tiny to stay operable.

blocks.subTitle: What to monitor
blocks.markdown:
Each pattern has a signal that screams when it breaks.

- **Fan-out queue depth** — growing means tweets aren't reaching timelines; watch p99 completion.
- **CDN cache-hit ratio** — a drop pushes traffic to origin, raising cost and latency.
- **Per-cell QPS** — a cell far above the median is a hotspot that will time out matches.
- **Duplicate-charge rate** — should be ~0; any nonzero value is a sev incident.
- **Scatter-gather tail latency** — the slowest shard drags the whole query ("tail at scale").

The misconceptions that sink interviews:

- **"Big companies have secret magic."** No — well-known patterns applied carefully. Give the *why*.
- **"Microservices beat monoliths."** Only past a scale; WhatsApp won going the other way.
- **"Fan-out-on-write is the Twitter answer."** It's the default; missing the celebrity hybrid is the classic trip-up.
- **"Idempotency = same response."** It means the same *effect* however many retries — not response caching.
- **"A ledger is just a transactions table."** It's append-only, double-entry, balances *derived* by summing.
